## Introduction:

This tutorial demonstrates how to process RRBS (Reduced Representation Bisulfite Sequencing) data using the methylKit package in R. We'll simulate RRBS-like data for human chromosome 17, process the data, perform differential methylation analysis, and then conduct sliding window analysis to detect DMRs (Differentially Methylated Regions).

## Package Installation and Loading

```{r, warning=F, message=F}
# Uncomment to install if not already installed
# install.packages("BiocManager")
# BiocManager::install("methylKit")
# BiocManager::install("pheatmap")
# install.packages("ggplot2")

library("methylKit")
library(pheatmap)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Grab sample data for RRBS

```{r}

# Use the pregenerated sample included in methylKit
set.seed(1337)

data(methylKit)

myobj <- methylRawList.obj
```

## Filter and Unite Methylation Calls

```{r}
# Filter CpGs with low coverage and high coverage outliers
filtered.myobj <- filterByCoverage(
  myobj, 
  lo.count = 10, lo.perc = NULL, 
  hi.count = NULL, hi.perc = 99.9
)

# Normalize coverage across samples
norm.myobj <- normalizeCoverage(filtered.myobj)

norm.myobj

# Unite methylation calls across samples
meth <- unite(norm.myobj, destrand = TRUE)

head(meth)
```

Should we filter and normalize before or after uniting?

**Filtering/Normalization before unite:** Each sample is filtered separately (e.g. remove low coverage CpGs sample-by-sample). Coverage normalization is applied to each sample’s methylation counts before combining. When you later unite(), only CpGs that pass filters across samples will be kept. This is the recommended approach in methylKit tutorials, because it ensures low-quality sites don’t make it into the combined dataset.

Use this when you want to be stricter about quality control and avoid bias from sites with poor coverage.

**Unite before filtering/normalization:** All CpGs across samples are combined first. Then you filter and normalize on the united dataset. This means some CpGs that had poor coverage in one sample (but good in another) might still be included in the combined matrix initially, only to be filtered later. It’s less strict and can sometimes leave slightly unbalanced coverage distributions before normalization.

This can be useful if you want to maximize the overlap of CpGs across samples before filtering, but it risks carrying noisier data into the merged set.

The methylKit authors recommend filtering and normalizing before uniting. That way each sample is cleaned up individually before being merged, which tends to give more reliable downstream results.

```{r}
# Clustering and PCA of samples
clusterSamples(meth, dist = "correlation", method = "ward", plot = TRUE)
PCASamples(meth)

# Percent methylation histogram for a sample
getMethylationStats(norm.myobj[[1]], plot = TRUE, both.strands = FALSE)

# Coverage histogram
getCoverageStats(norm.myobj[[1]], plot = TRUE, both.strands = FALSE)
getCoverageStats(norm.myobj[[2]], plot = TRUE, both.strands = FALSE)
getCoverageStats(norm.myobj[[3]], plot = TRUE, both.strands = FALSE)
getCoverageStats(norm.myobj[[4]], plot = TRUE, both.strands = FALSE)

```

## Differential Methylation Analysis (CpG-Level)

```{r}
# Run logistic regression based test
myDiff <- calculateDiffMeth(meth)

# Extract significant DMRs (q < 0.01, methylation diff > 25%)
sigDiff <- getMethylDiff(myDiff, qvalue = 0.01, difference = 25)

# View top results
head(sigDiff)
```

## What is q-value and why do we use the cutoffs that we use?

When methylKit tests for differential methylation at each CpG or region, it calculates a p-value for the null hypothesis “no difference between groups.”

But we’re testing hundreds of thousands (CpGs) or tens of thousands (windows) of sites.

If we used plain p-values (say cutoff 0.05), we would get thousands of false positives just by chance. To correct for this, methylKit adjusts the p-values using multiple testing correction (by default: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR).

The adjusted p-value is called a q-value (false discovery rate–adjusted p-value).

**Interpretation:**

A q-value of 0.01 means that, on average, 1% of the significant calls are expected to be false positives.

**Why use a cutoff of q = 0.01?**

q = 0.05 is common in genomics, but can still yield a lot of false positives when testing millions of CpGs. q = 0.01 is stricter. It reduces false positives, making our DMR list more reliable.

It’s a balance: Lower q-value cutoff (0.01) = fewer but more confident DMRs Higher q-value cutoff (0.05, 0.1) = more DMRs, but more likely to include false calls

We often use q = 0.01 to highlight clear, confident results without being overwhelmed with noise. We may wish to try 0.05 if we want to be less stringent

**Why do we use a difference cutoff?**

Above we used a difference of 25%. Methylation values are often measured as beta values, which is a value between 0-1, representing the percentage of methylation within your sample at that site. A 25% cutoff also allows us to find biologically meaningful results, as low sample numbers can impact the Inter-quartile range or standard deviation (metrics used for statistical testing). Some studies will use 20%.

## Visualize the DMA

```{r}

# Methylation difference per chromosome (should show only chr21)
diffMethPerChr(myDiff, plot = TRUE, qvalue.cutoff = 0.01, meth.cutoff = 25)



# Top 100 CpGs
top_rows <- 1:min(100, nrow(sigDiff))  # adjust if fewer than 100
meth_top <- meth[top_rows, ]

# Percent methylation matrix
mat <- percMethylation(meth_top)

# Remove rows with NA
mat <- mat[complete.cases(mat), ]

# Remove rows with zero variance (all samples identical)
mat <- mat[apply(mat, 1, var) > 0, ]

# Plot heatmap
pheatmap(mat,
         scale = "row",
         clustering_distance_rows = "correlation",
         clustering_distance_cols = "euclidean",
         main = "Heatmap of Top Differentially Methylated CpGs")

cat("Number of CpGs plotted:", nrow(mat), "out of", nrow(meth_top), "\n")

```

## Sliding Window Analysis (DMR Detection)

```{r}

# Tile chromosome 21 into 1000 bp windows
tiles <- tileMethylCounts(norm.myobj, win.size = 1000, step.size = 1000)

# Unite tiled data across samples
tiles.united <- unite(tiles, destrand = TRUE)

# Perform differential methylation on windows
tiles.diff <- calculateDiffMeth(tiles.united)

# Extract significant window-level differences
sigTiles <- getMethylDiff(tiles.diff, qvalue = 0.01, difference = 25)

head(sigTiles)

```

## Visualize the DMRs

```{r}

# Plot DMRs across chr17
diffMethPerChr(tiles.diff, plot = TRUE)

df <- as.data.frame(tiles.diff)
ggplot(df, aes(x = meth.diff, y = -log10(qvalue))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-25, 25), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.01), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Volcano Plot of Differential Methylation Regions",
       x = "Methylation Difference (%)",
       y = "-log10(q-value)") +
  theme_minimal()

df$chr <- factor(df$chr, levels = unique(df$chr))  # preserve chr order
ggplot(df, aes(x = start, y = -log10(qvalue), color = chr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Manhattan Plot of DMRs",
       x = "Genomic Position",
       y = "-log10(q-value)") +
  theme_minimal()


# Select top 50 significant tiles (or fewer if dataset is small)
sigTiles50 <- getMethylDiff(tiles.diff, qvalue = 0.01, difference = 25)
top_rows <- 1:min(50, nrow(sigTiles50))
tiles_top <- tiles.united[top_rows, ]

mat_tiles <- percMethylation(tiles_top)

# Remove rows with NA
mat_tiles <- mat_tiles[complete.cases(mat_tiles), ]

# Remove rows with zero variance (all samples identical)
mat_tiles <- mat_tiles[apply(mat_tiles, 1, var) > 0, ]

# Plot heatmap
pheatmap(mat_tiles,
         scale = "row",
         clustering_distance_rows = "correlation",
         clustering_distance_cols = "euclidean",
         main = "Heatmap of Top Differentially Methylated Windows")

cat("Number of regions plotted:", nrow(mat_tiles), "out of", nrow(tiles_top ), "\n")

```

## Export the results

```{r}

# Convert sigDiff to BED format
bed.gr <- as(sigDiff, "GRanges")

# Save as BED file
rtracklayer::export(bed.gr, "CpG_DMRs_chr21.bed")

# Check
head(bed.gr)

# Export DMR results to BED format
tile.gr <- as(sigTiles, "GRanges")
rtracklayer::export(tile.gr, "Window_DMRs_chr21.bed")

# Export to CSV for further analysis

# CpG-level
write.csv(as.data.frame(sigDiff), "CpG_DMRs_chr21.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Window-level
write.csv(as.data.frame(sigTiles), "Window_DMRs_chr21.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

## Comparing CpG-level vs Window-level DMRs

You may have noticed that there is a difference between the hypo/hyper methylation if we look at sites vs regions. Now let’s explore why the proportions of hyper- vs hypo-methylated regions can differ between CpG-level and region-level analyses.

```{r}

library(GenomicRanges)

# --- 1) counts and proportions at CpG and window level

# get significant lists (use same thresholds we used for plotting)
sigDiff <- getMethylDiff(myDiff, qvalue = 0.01, difference = 25)
sigTiles <- getMethylDiff(tiles.diff, qvalue = 0.01, difference = 25)

# counts & proportions
cpg_hyper <- nrow(getMethylDiff(myDiff, qvalue=0.01, difference=25, type="hyper"))
cpg_hypo  <- nrow(getMethylDiff(myDiff, qvalue=0.01, difference=25, type="hypo"))
cpg_total <- cpg_hyper + cpg_hypo
cat("CpG DMCs: hyper =", cpg_hyper, " hypo =", cpg_hypo, " total =", cpg_total, "\n")
cat("CpG proportions: hyper%", 100*cpg_hyper/cpg_total, " hypo%", 100*cpg_hypo/cpg_total, "\n\n")

tile_hyper <- nrow(getMethylDiff(tiles.diff, qvalue=0.01, difference=25, type="hyper"))
tile_hypo  <- nrow(getMethylDiff(tiles.diff, qvalue=0.01, difference=25, type="hypo"))
tile_total <- tile_hyper + tile_hypo
cat("Tile DMRs: hyper =", tile_hyper, " hypo =", tile_hypo, " total =", tile_total, "\n")
cat("Tile proportions: hyper%", 100*tile_hyper/tile_total, " hypo%", 100*tile_hypo/tile_total, "\n\n")

# --- 2) Compare number of tests (affects FDR)
num_tests_cpg   <- nrow(as.data.frame(myDiff))    # total CpG entries tested
num_tests_tiles <- nrow(as.data.frame(tiles.diff))# total windows tested
cat("Number tested: CpGs =", num_tests_cpg, " windows =", num_tests_tiles, "\n\n")

# --- 3) Overlap CpG-level DMRs with window-level DMRs, and check direction concordance
gr_cpg   <- as(sigDiff, "GRanges")
gr_tiles <- as(sigTiles, "GRanges")

# find overlaps
ov <- findOverlaps(gr_tiles, gr_cpg)
cat("Number of overlapping tile<->CpG pairs:", length(ov), "\n")

# For each overlap check directionality: methylKit stores methylation difference in 'meth.diff'
cpg_df   <- as.data.frame(sigDiff)    # should include 'meth.diff' (mean difference)
tile_df  <- as.data.frame(sigTiles)

# Map overlaps: tile i overlaps some CpG j
tile_idx <- queryHits(ov)
cpg_idx  <- subjectHits(ov)

# Are directions concordant?
concordant <- sum(sign(tile_df$meth.diff[tile_idx]) == sign(cpg_df$meth.diff[cpg_idx]))
discordant  <- length(ov) - concordant
cat("Overlapping pairs concordant:", concordant, " discordant:", discordant, "\n\n")

# --- 4) For tiles that are significant, inspect distribution of CpG-level diffs inside each tile
# get all tiled CpGs (not only significant ones) to see averaging effect:
# We'll need the tiled methylRawList used to create tiles to get per-sample CpG info
# but a simpler approach: compute mean CpG diff per tile by overlapping ALL CpG diffs
allCpGdf <- as.data.frame(myDiff)  # includes all CpG diff tests, not only significant
allCpGgr <- GRanges(seqnames=allCpGdf$chr,
                    ranges=IRanges(start=allCpGdf$start, end=allCpGdf$end),
                    meth.diff = allCpGdf$meth.diff)

# Use findOverlaps to aggregate per tile
ov_all <- findOverlaps(gr_tiles, allCpGgr)
tile_to_cpgs <- split(subjectHits(ov_all), queryHits(ov_all))

# compute mean CpG diffs for each significant tile
mean_cpg_diff_per_tile <- sapply(names(tile_to_cpgs), function(i){
  idxs <- tile_to_cpgs[[i]]
  mean(allCpGdf$meth.diff[idxs], na.rm=TRUE)
})
# compare to tile-level reported meth.diff
tile_reported_diff <- tile_df$meth.diff
cat("\nSummary of (Region reported mean diff) - (mean of individual CpG diffs):\n")
print(summary(tile_reported_diff - mean_cpg_diff_per_tile))

# --- 5) Check CpG counts per tile (density) — low-count tiles are noisier
cpg_counts <- sapply(tile_to_cpgs, length)
cat("\nSummary of the CPG counts per Region: \n")
summary(cpg_counts)

```

## What does this tell us?

We can see that the sites and regions are in complete concordance with one another, however, we see a stark difference in median and mean CpG counts per region. This tells use that the distribution of CpG sites across the regions are quite skewed. When looking at the difference of differences, we can see that median and mean are close to 0, however, the overall distribution seems a bit skewed.

As such, single-CpG level hypo/hyper methylation is possible to calculate with MethylKit, however, it is not ideal. While there is strong (100%) agreement with region level hypo/hyper methylation, the region level analysis provides a more biologically relevant answer.

Regions can also be done using predefined regions, such as promoter regions.

In short, when doing hypo/hyper methylation analysis, the biological interpretation is done at the regional level. This is because single-site calls can be noisy. There are other situations where one would prefer a single-site analysis, but we may wish to use an array (such as EPIC) for such an analysis (Less cost).
